{{Short description|Surjective ring homomorphism with a given codomain}}
{{hat note|For the ring-theoretic equivalent of a [[field extension]], see [[Subring#Ring extension]].}}
{{confused|Algebraic extension}}

In [[abstract algebra]], an '''algebra extension''' is the ring-theoretic equivalent of a [[group extension]].

Precisely, a '''ring extension''' of a [[ring (mathematics)|ring]] ''R'' by an [[abelian group]] ''I'' is a pair (''E'', <math> \phi </math>) consisting of a ring ''E'' and a [[ring homomorphism]] <math> \phi </math> that fits into the [[short exact sequence]] of abelian groups:
:<math>0 \to I \to E \overset{\phi}{{}\to{}} R \to 0.</math><ref name="Sernesi">{{harvnb|Sernesi|2007|loc=1.1.1.}}</ref>
This makes ''I''  isomorphic to a [[Ideal (ring theory)|two-sided ideal]] of ''E''.

Given a [[commutative ring]] ''A'', an '''''A''-extension''' or an '''extension of an ''A''-algebra''' is defined in the same way by replacing "ring" with "[[Algebra over a field#Generalization: algebra over a ring|algebra]] over ''A''" and "abelian groups" with "''A''-[[Module (mathematics)|modules]]".

An extension is said to be ''trivial'' or to ''split'' if <math> \phi </math> splits; i.e., <math> \phi </math> admits a [[Section (category theory)|section]] that is a [[ring homomorphism]]<ref>Typical references require sections be homomorphisms without elaborating whether 1 is preserved. But since we need to be able to identify ''R'' as a subring of ''E'' (see the trivial extension example), it seems 1 needs to be preserved.</ref> (see {{section link||Example: trivial extension}}).

A [[morphism]] between extensions of ''R'' by ''I'', over say ''A'', is an algebra homomorphism ''E'' → ''E{{'}}'' that induces the identities on ''I'' and ''R''. By the [[five lemma]], such a morphism is necessarily an [[isomorphism]], and so two extensions are equivalent if there is a morphism between them.<!-- the reference only consider module extensions, I think. There is a natural bijection between the set of the equivalence classes of the extensions of ''R'' by ''I'' and the [[Ext group]] <math>\operatorname{Ext}^1_A(R, I)/math>.<ref>Exercise A 3.26. of [[David Eisenbud|Eisenbud, David]], ''Commutative Algebra with a View Toward Algebraic Geometry'', Graduate Texts in Mathematics, 150, Springer-Verlag, 1995, ISBN 0-387-94268-8.</ref>-->

== Trivial extension example ==
<!-- The following example seems a special case of the next example
===Example 1===
Let's take the ring <math>\mathbb Z</math> of whole numbers and let's take the abelian group <math>\mathbb Z_2</math>(under addition) of binary numbers. Let ''E'' = <math>\mathbb Z \oplus \mathbb Z_2</math> we can identify multiplication on ''E'' by <math>(x,a) \cdot (y,b) = (xy,\phi(x)a+\phi(y)b)</math>(where <math>\phi:\mathbb Z \to \mathbb Z_2</math> is the homomorphism mapping even numbers to 0 and odd numbers to 1).
This gives the short exact sequence
:<math>0\to \mathbb Z \to E \overset{p}{{}\to{}} \mathbb Z \to 0</math>
Where ''p'' is the homomorphism mapping <math>(x,a) \mapsto a\phi(x)</math>.{{disputed inline|reason=as  it is, this is completely wrong|date=February 2023}}

===Example 2===-->
Let ''R'' be a commutative ring and ''M'' an ''R''-module. Let ''E'' = ''R'' ⊕ ''M'' be the [[Direct sum#Direct sum of abelian groups|direct sum]] of abelian groups. Define the multiplication on ''E'' by
:<math>(a, x) \cdot (b, y) = (ab, ay + bx).</math>
Note that identifying (''a'', ''x'') with ''a'' + ''εx'' where ε squares to zero and expanding out (''a'' + ''εx'')(''b'' + ''εy'') yields the above formula; in particular we see that ''E'' is a ring. It is sometimes called the '''algebra of dual numbers'''. Alternatively, ''E'' can be defined as <math>\operatorname{Sym}(M)/\bigoplus_{n \ge 2} \operatorname{Sym}^n(M)</math> where <math>\operatorname{Sym}(M)</math> is the [[symmetric algebra]] of ''M''.<ref>{{cite journal |last1=Anderson |first1=D. D. |last2=Winders |first2=M. |title=Idealization of a Module |journal=Journal of Commutative Algebra |date=March 2009 |volume=1 |issue=1 |pages=3–56 |doi=10.1216/JCA-2009-1-1-3 |s2cid=120720674 |issn=1939-2346|doi-access=free }}</ref> We then have the short exact sequence
:<math>0 \to M \to E \overset{p}{{}\to{}} R \to 0</math>
where ''p'' is the projection. Hence, ''E'' is an extension of ''R'' by ''M''. It is trivial since <math>r \mapsto (r, 0)</math> is a section (note this section is a ring homomorphism since <math>(1, 0)</math> is the multiplicative identity of ''E''). Conversely, every trivial extension ''E'' of ''R'' by ''I'' is isomorphic to <math>R \oplus I</math> if <math>I^2 = 0</math>. Indeed, identifying <math>R</math> as a subring of ''E'' using a section, we have <math>(E, \phi) \simeq (R \oplus I, p)</math> via <math>e \mapsto (\phi(e), e - \phi(e))</math>.<ref name="Sernesi" />

One interesting feature of this construction is that the module ''M'' becomes an ideal of some new ring. In his book ''Local Rings'', [[Masayoshi Nagata|Nagata]] calls this process the ''principle of idealization''.<ref>{{citation|mr=0155856|last=Nagata|first=Masayoshi|author-link=Masayoshi Nagata|title=Local Rings|series=Interscience Tracts in Pure and Applied Mathematics|volume=13|publisher=Interscience Publishers a division of John Wiley & Sons|place=New York-London|year=1962|isbn=0-88275-228-6}}</ref>

== Square-zero extension ==
{{expand section|date=March 2023}}
Especially in [[deformation theory]], it is common to consider an extension ''R'' of a ring (commutative or not) by an ideal whose square is zero. Such an extension is called a '''square-zero extension''', a square extension or just an extension. For a square-zero ideal ''I'', since ''I'' is contained in the left and right annihilators of itself, ''I'' is a <math>R/I</math>-bimodule.

More generally, an extension by a nilpotent ideal is called a '''nilpotent extension'''. For example, the quotient <math>R \to R_{\mathrm{red}}</math> of a Noetherian commutative ring by the nilradical is a nilpotent extension.

In general,
:<math>0 \to I^n/I^{n-1} \to R/I^{n-1} \to R/I^n \to 0</math>
is a square-zero extension. Thus, a nilpotent extension breaks up into successive square-zero extensions. Because of this, it is usually enough to study square-zero extensions in order to understand nilpotent extensions.
